title: If I'm Wrong About AI in Education, Here's Why
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Meyer pre-registers three falsifiable bets against the large claims made for AI chatbots in education within five years: no peer-reviewed replication of Bloom's two-sigma tutoring effect, no survey in which most students prefer a chatbot to their classroom teacher, and no attributable change in hiring or attrition in the largest districts. Each bet is supported by his view that learning gains need tutors who are consistent and relational, and that teacher satisfaction depends on factors chatbots do not touch. He adds a pre-mortem of how he could be wrong. His central claim is that the safest bet in education is the status quo and that AI will deliver modest quality-of-life improvements, not transformation. It is Ed-Tech because the role of AI in schools is the whole subject.
points: Bet one holds that no study will replicate the two-sigma effect with AI tutors, since that effect needs a consistent, relational tutor.
Students who need tutoring need the tutor to be right, so asking them to correct a hallucinating chatbot only works for students who do not need one.
Where students can access both a teacher and a chatbot, they will choose human relationship in learning.
Teacher attrition is driven by resources, respect, climate, collaboration and development, none of which chatbots address.
The most optimistic outcome is quality-of-life improvements like a grammar checker, with those helping kids learn through relationship told to stay their course.
quotes: My perspective has been “no, I don't think so,” to all of the above and history is on my side here. With the exception of huge exogenous events like a global pandemic or recession, etc, the safest bet in education, for better or worse, has always been the status quo.

First, these chatbots are wrong at rates most people would find unacceptable for human tutors. Some people try to convert this lack of reliability and validity into a meta-cognitive exercise for students—correct the tutor!—but that exercise is only productive or interesting to students who don’t need a tutor. Students who need a tutor need the tutor to be right.

My premise here is that anything close to a two-sigma improvement in learning requires a tutor that is consistent and relational. Someone who knows to follow up on your last exam. Someone who will encourage, push, and pull you beyond what you think are your limits. People are not anywhere close to forming those kinds of relationships with AI chatbots.

I find it plausible that students would prefer a chatbot in situations where their class is staffed by substitute teachers or no teacher at all. But in situations where students have access to a classroom teacher and a chatbot, you won’t find even a plurality of them claim to prefer the chatbot to the human.

Some commenters have suggested that AI chatbots will help us retain teachers by functioning as teaching assistants. But I don’t think we will see that effect, mainly because AI chatbots are irrelevant to the largest factors contributing to job satisfaction among teachers: resource availability, professional respect, disciplinary climate, self-efficacy, teacher collaboration, professional development opportunities (see pp 81-84).

The most optimistic outcome I can conjure for AI in education is that it will manifest as a series of quality-of-life improvements for teachers and students, similar to the AI grammar checker that is right now ensuring I maintain subject-verb agreement, but not much more than that. I like that grammar checker, but it has not substantially changed how I write and likewise AI will not substantially change how kids learn new ideas.
So if you are, right now, helping kids learn through social relationship, I encourage you to stay your course because it is the only course that matters.
